claims.text: Chemical disorder and differences in constituent atomic radii produce local lattice distortions in high-entropy solid solutions.
Local lattice distortions modulate electron–phonon coupling in superconducting high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions modulate the electronic density of states at the Fermi level in superconducting high-entropy alloys.
Changes in electron–phonon coupling affect the superconducting transition temperature.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level affect the superconducting transition temperature.
A high-entropy alloy can be defined as containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 atomic percent each.
The proposed baseline is a single-phase Nb–Ta-based high-entropy solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
A Nb–Ta-based high-entropy alloy has a known superconducting transition temperature.
Substituting constituents with elements of different atomic radii can vary local lattice distortion.
Maintaining comparable valence-electron counts and phase purity is intended to isolate lattice distortion as the principal experimental variable.
The substituted alloy should exhibit a measurable change in superconducting transition temperature relative to the baseline.
The transition-temperature change should be accompanied by spectroscopic signatures of altered electron–phonon interactions.
The direction and magnitude of the transition-temperature shift may be nonlinear and dependent on the substituted elements.
The proposed interpretation applies only if the modified compositions remain single-phase solid solutions without important changes in valence-electron count.
Transition temperature can be compared between baseline and modified samples using resistivity or magnetic-susceptibility measurements under identical cryogenic conditions.
A reproducible absence of correlation between structurally confirmed lattice-distortion changes and both transition temperature and relevant spectroscopic signatures would falsify the hypothesis.
